evidence.claim: Farmland roads link old mill communities and a colonial meetinghouse
evidence.quote: Visitors who travel the Upper Freehold Historic Farmland Scenic Byway can visit the historic places in the picturesque Borough of Allentown, the pristine farmland of historic Upper Freehold Township, Historic Walnford, the Old Yellow Meeting House and the hamlet of Imlaystown.

evidence.claim: The Upper Freehold Historic Farmland Scenic Byway links Allentown with farmland and mill communities in Monmouth County.
evidence.quote: The Upper Freehold Historic Farmland Byway runs through areas of farmland between Allentown and Walnford in Monmouth County.

evidence.claim: The drive follows county and local roads, including Rues Road and Red Valley Road.
evidence.quote: The byway follows CR 539, CR 524, Chambers Road, Rues Road, CR 526, Red Valley Road

evidence.claim: New Jersey DOT identifies history and culture as the scenic byway’s defining qualities and describes a corridor where agricultural traditions remain visible.
evidence.quote: captures the unique agricultural, historical, environmental and cultural traditions still visible in the area around Upper Freehold and Allentown.

evidence.claim: Its published length is approximately 24 miles.
evidence.quote: Length: Approximately 24 miles

evidence.claim: The roads connect settlements shaped by farming and milling.
evidence.quote: runs through areas of farmland between Allentown and Walnford

evidence.claim: At Walnford, Philadelphia merchant Richard Waln bought several mills in 1772 and built a house the following year.
evidence.quote: In 1772, Richard Waln (1737–1809), a Philadelphia merchant, purchased several mills in the area, which he then named Walnford. He built a two and one-half story house here in 1773.

evidence.claim: The road network changed: two sections of Walnford Road that once joined now require a circuit through other roads to reach the mill.
evidence.quote: Take Polhemustown Road and make a right onto Holmes Mill Road. Follow Holmes Mill Road to Walnford Road and make another right. These two sections of Walnford Road were once connected. Follow Walnford Road until it deadends at the Walnford Mill.

evidence.claim: Following DOT’s detailed tour, begin at Allentown’s Presbyterian Church and head out along Main Street toward Chambers Road and Rues Road.
evidence.quote: Start at the Presbyterian Church on Route 539 (High Street) and travel northwest. Turn right onto Route 524/539 (Main Street/Old York Road). Continue northeast and turn right onto Route 524 (New Canton-Stone Tavern Road) to Chambers Road and make a right. Travel south on Chambers Road and make another right onto Rues Road.

evidence.claim: Route 526 leads toward Red Valley Road, with a northward spur to the Old Yellow Meeting House.
evidence.quote: Take Route 526 to Red Valley Road and make a right. Spur to Old Yellow Meeting House - from Route 526 make a left onto Yellow Meeting House Road and travel north until Old Yellow Meeting House on left.

evidence.claim: Continue by Holmes Mill Road and Arneytown-Hornerstown Road to Hill Road, then cross Crosswicks Creek on the old iron bridge.
evidence.quote: Follow Route 27 (Holmes Mill Road) and turn right onto Arneytown-Hornerstown Road. Follow Arneytown-Hornerstown Road to Hill Road and turn right again. Travel north on Hill Road. At the intersection of Waln’s Mill Road (Walnford Road) turn right and cross over Crosswicks Creek on the old iron bridge.

evidence.claim: The final approach ends at Walnford Mill.
evidence.quote: Follow Walnford Road until it deadends at the Walnford Mill.

evidence.claim: history and culture as the scenic byway’s defining qualities
evidence.quote: Intrinsic qualities: Historical and cultural

evidence.claim: A 28-acre millpond served two businesses in Imlaystown: milling and ice.
evidence.quote: Salter's Mill situated on a 28-acre (110,000 m2) millpond that once supported an ice business as well as the mill.

evidence.claim: The community dates to 1690 and takes its name from the Imlay family, major colonial landowners.
evidence.quote: Founded in 1690, the community was once the social, economic and political focus of Upper Freehold.

evidence.claim: Much of the town was rebuilt in 1898 after a destructive fire.
evidence.quote: Most were rebuilt in 1898 after a fire which destroyed much of the town.

evidence.claim: Salter’s Mill also replaced an earlier mill damaged by fire, and its two-and-a-half-story frame building contains a horizontal turbine wheel.
evidence.quote: It was badly damaged by a fire in 1897 and the current mill was built soon afterwards. The two and one-half story frame building has a horizontal turbine wheel.

evidence.claim: The Golden family closed milling operations in 1962; the millpond was restored in 1995.
evidence.quote: The last owner was the Golden family, who closed mill operations in 1962.

evidence.claim: Salter’s Mill stands beside the 28-acre millpond.
evidence.quote: The mill is next to a 28-acre (11 ha) mill pond

evidence.claim: takes its name from the Imlay family, major colonial landowners
evidence.quote: It takes its name from the Imlay family, the area's major landowners in the colonial period.

evidence.claim: the millpond was restored in 1995
evidence.quote: including the restoration of the millpond in 1995

evidence.claim: The meetinghouse’s gable ends face east and west, an arrangement intended to maximize sunlight on its southern side.
evidence.quote: It is oriented so that the gable ends are facing due east and west, to maximize sunlight on the southern side.

evidence.claim: An earlier Baptist meeting building went up in 1720 on land Thomas and Rachel Salter donated.
evidence.quote: An earlier building for the area Baptists was erected in 1720 on land donated by Thomas and Rachel Salter.

evidence.claim: The present meetinghouse followed in 1737.
evidence.quote: The current meeting house was built in 1737.

evidence.claim: The cemetery preserves an earlier date: its oldest dated grave belongs to their son John, who died on August 29, 1723.
evidence.quote: The oldest dated grave in the Yellow Meeting House Cemetery is Salter's son, John, who died August 29, 1723.

evidence.claim: The byway’s spur reaches the meetinghouse north of Route 526 on Yellow Meeting House Road.
evidence.quote: from Route 526 make a left onto Yellow Meeting House Road and travel north until Old Yellow Meeting House on left.

evidence.claim: The gable ends face east and west.
evidence.quote: the gable ends are facing due east and west

evidence.claim: Walnford’s gristmill stands on Crosswicks Creek, within a historic district that also includes Richard Waln’s 1773 house.
evidence.quote: It features the house built by Richard Waln in 1773, and the grist mill on Crosswicks Creek.

evidence.claim: Waln was a Philadelphia merchant who bought several mills here in 1772 and gave the settlement its name.
evidence.quote: In 1772, Richard Waln (1737–1809), a Philadelphia merchant, purchased several mills in the area, which he then named Walnford.

evidence.claim: His son Nicolas inherited the property, and descendants lived here for nearly 200 years.
evidence.quote: The property was inherited by his son, Nicolas Waln, and his descendants continued to live here for nearly 200 years.

evidence.claim: The preserved complex includes a carriage house and cow barn as well as the restored Georgian house and mill.
evidence.quote: Historic Walnford includes a restored Georgian style house, working mill, carriage house and cow barn

evidence.claim: Walnford Road ends at the mill.
evidence.quote: Follow Walnford Road until it deadends at the Walnford Mill.

evidence.claim: The gristmill sits on Crosswicks Creek; the historic district also includes Waln’s 1773 house.
evidence.quote: It features the house built by Richard Waln in 1773, and the grist mill on Crosswicks Creek.

evidence.claim: Allentown and Imlaystown are historic districts within the corridor, and the neighboring farms have been here for multiple generations.
evidence.quote: Two historic districts - Allentown and Imlaystown - are located within the Upper Freehold Historic Farmland Scenic Byway corridor

evidence.claim: the neighboring farms have been here for multiple generations
evidence.quote: Many of the neighboring farms have been here for multiple generations.

evidence.claim: An optional return from the mill takes drivers back through Holmes Mill Road toward Allentown.
evidence.quote: To complete the loop go back out to Holmes Mill Road and make a left.

evidence.claim: toward Allentown
evidence.quote: takes you back into Allentown.

evidence.claim: The historic district also includes a two-story brick school built in 1930 in the Colonial Revival style.
evidence.quote: The two-story brick school building was constructed in 1930 with Colonial Revival style.

evidence.claim: The congregation’s first resident minister was David Jones; the meetinghouse is the oldest Baptist meetinghouse in New Jersey.
evidence.quote: The first resident minister for the congregation was David Jones (1736–1820).

evidence.claim: the oldest Baptist meetinghouse in New Jersey
evidence.quote: It is the oldest Baptist meetinghouse in the state.

evidence.claim: The district entered the National Register of Historic Places in 1976 for its significance in agriculture and commerce.
evidence.quote: It was added to the National Register of Historic Places on June 29, 1976 for its significance in agriculture and commerce.

flags: NJDOT’s route summary starts at Walnford and ends at Polhemustown Road/539, but its detailed tour begins at Allentown and ends at Walnford before an optional return. Story follows the detailed tour and material driving order, not a definitive endpoint claim.
Cache gives little road construction or designation history, grades or driving time; the shorter overview uses the documented divided Walnford Road and mill settlement history.
The town article gives 1898 for rebuilding after fire; the mill article gives 1897 for mill fire damage. They are not treated as one dated event.

Dropped current claim that the same families have worked the farms for generations: NJDOT says neighboring farms have existed for multiple generations, not that ownership or labor has remained in the same families.
